intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a geology professor.

turns.text: Professor Brandt, could I run my paper topic by you? I'm thinking of writing about how volcanic soils affect farming around the world.
Around the world? In twelve pages?
Well, I know it's big. But there's so much good material, and I didn't want to leave anything out.
That's the trouble, though. If you cover everything, you can only say a sentence or two about each place. Is there a region you've read a lot about?
Actually, yes. Coffee farms on volcanic slopes in Central America. And I found a few studies on rice terraces in Southeast Asia.
Now that could work. Two regions, two very different crops, the same kind of soil. You'd have room to really compare them.
So I'd drop the global part completely?
Mention it in your introduction, as background. Send me a revised outline by Friday.

questions.prompt: Why does the student go to see the professor?
options: To get feedback on a topic for a paper
To ask for more pages for her paper
To request studies about rice farming
To hand in a revised paper outline
questions.explanation: She asks the professor to look at her paper topic on volcanic soils and farming.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about the student's original plan?
options: It would require sources she cannot find.
It leaves out the most important crops.
It repeats a topic from an earlier class.
It would make her discussion too shallow.
questions.explanation: He says covering everything would leave only a sentence or two for each place.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teaching assistant for a chemistry course.

turns.text: Hi, Aisha. Do you have a second? I got my lab report back, and I lost fifteen points. I'm not sure why.
Sure, let me see. Oh, right. Your results section is fine, but you didn't include any error analysis.
Error analysis? I thought that was only for the final report.
No, it's required for every report this semester. It was in the guidelines. You need to estimate how uncertain your measurements were, like the readings from the balance.
Oh, I must have missed that. Is there anything I can do now?
The professor lets students revise one report per term. If you add the error analysis and turn it in by Monday, you can earn back up to ten points.
Great. I'll work on it this weekend.
Good. And check the example report that's posted online. It shows the format we want.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: How to read a laboratory balance correctly
When the final lab report is due
Whether the course guidelines have changed
Why points were taken off a lab report
questions.explanation: The student asks why he lost fifteen points, and the assistant explains the missing error analysis.

questions.prompt: What can the student do to improve his grade?
options: Repeat the experiment over the weekend
Add the missing section and resubmit the report
Ask the professor to drop his lowest score
Turn in an extra report before the final
questions.explanation: She says he can add the error analysis by Monday and earn back up to ten points.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and an astronomy professor.

turns.text: Professor Ruiz, I'm sorry I missed the observing session on Tuesday night. I had a swim meet out of town. Is there a make-up session?
I wish there were. The point was to sketch the moon at first quarter, when the crater shadows are longest. That won't happen again for a month, and by then we'll be on to planets.
So I just lose the points?
Not necessarily. The department keeps an archive of telescope images taken at that same phase. You could measure the shadows from a photo and estimate the crater depths the same way.
That sounds like more work than sketching through the telescope.
Probably a bit more, yes. But it's the same skill. Next time, though, tell me before you miss a session.
I will. Where do I find the archive?

questions.prompt: Why does the student go to see the professor?
options: To ask about joining a trip out of town
To borrow a telescope for a few nights
To find out how to make up missed work
To ask about the next unit on planets
questions.explanation: He missed the observing session and asks whether there is a way to make it up.

questions.prompt: What is the professor's attitude toward the alternative assignment?
options: She thinks it is easier than the original task.
She doubts the archive has suitable images.
She admits it is harder but considers it fair.
She feels it will not teach the same skill.
questions.explanation: She agrees it is a bit more work but says it practices the same skill.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a sociology professor.

turns.text: Professor Hale, I'm planning my project on why some commuter students don't join campus clubs. I was going to use an online survey.
How many students do you think you'll reach?
Honestly, maybe fifteen. I only know a few commuters, and they'd have to pass it along.
With fifteen responses, a survey won't tell you much. The percentages would jump around too much. But fifteen is plenty for interviews.
Interviews? Wouldn't those take a lot longer?
Each one, yes. But you'd learn the reasons behind their choices, like work schedules or long drives. A survey would just turn those into checkboxes.
That makes sense. Should I write the questions first?
Yes. Draft about six open-ended questions and bring them to my office hours on Thursday.

questions.prompt: What are the speakers mainly discussing?
options: Which research method suits the student's project
Why commuter students rarely join campus clubs
How to send an online survey to more commuter students
When the student's project needs to be finished
questions.explanation: The professor explains why interviews would work better than a survey for her small group.

questions.prompt: What will the student probably do next?
options: Write a set of open-ended questions
Send an online survey to commuters
Join a club for commuting students
Choose a new topic for her project
questions.explanation: The professor tells her to draft six open-ended questions for Thursday, and she agrees.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teaching assistant for an economics course.

turns.text: Hi, Mei. I wanted to ask about question three on the midterm. I drew the supply shift correctly, but I only got half credit.
Let me look. Hmm, your curve moves the right way, but you didn't label the new equilibrium price.
Right, but the question only asked which direction the price would go. I wrote 'price rises' underneath.
I see that. The rubric we used says the label is required for full credit, though.
The question doesn't say anything about labels. I checked.
Okay, you have a point. I didn't write the rubric, so I can't change it on my own. But I'll show your exam to Professor Grant at our meeting tomorrow.
Thanks. I'm not trying to argue about every point. That one just seemed unfair.
No, it's a reasonable question. I'll email you after the meeting.

questions.prompt: Why does the student talk to the teaching assistant?
options: To learn how to label an equilibrium price
To question how one of his answers was scored
To find out when the exams will be returned
To ask for a meeting with Professor Grant
questions.explanation: He believes he lost credit on question three for something the question did not ask for.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the teaching assistant?
options: She believes the rubric was written carefully.
She plans to raise the student's score on her own.
She thinks the student's complaint may be valid.
She considers the student's request excessive.
questions.explanation: She admits he has a point and agrees to show his exam to the professor.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a linguistics professor.

turns.text: Dr. Varga, I'd like to do an independent study next semester. My grandmother's village has its own dialect, and fewer people speak it every year.
That's a wonderful idea. Have you recorded any speakers yet?
Just my grandmother, over the summer. About three hours.

That's a good start. For an independent study, though, the department needs a written proposal. You'd describe what you plan to analyze, maybe the vowel sounds or the vocabulary, and include a reading list.
How long should it be?
Two or three pages is fine. The deadline is the end of this month, and I'd be happy to supervise.
Really? Thank you. I'll start on the reading list this week.
Good. I'll send you a few articles on documenting dialects to get you going.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: Recording a grandmother's stories for a class
Choosing readings for a course on vowels
Finding speakers for a language experiment
Arranging an independent study of a dialect
questions.explanation: The student wants an independent study on his grandmother's village dialect, and the professor explains the requirements.

questions.prompt: What does the professor say the student must do?
options: Record several more speakers before applying
Submit a short written proposal by the deadline
Find another professor to supervise him
Complete a course on dialects beforehand
questions.explanation: She says the department needs a two- or three-page proposal by the end of the month.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a biology professor.

turns.text: Professor Abara, I'm applying to a summer research program at a marine station, and I was hoping you could write me a recommendation letter.
I'd be glad to help. Remind me, you took my genetics lecture last spring?
Yes, I got an A. And this year I've been working in Dr. Petrova's lab, collecting water samples.

Hmm. Well, I can certainly say you did excellent work on exams. But the program will want to know how you handle fieldwork and lab routines. Dr. Petrova has seen that firsthand. I only saw you in a lecture hall of two hundred.
Oh. I just thought a letter from a full professor might carry more weight.
Titles matter less than details. Ask her first. If they need a second letter, I'm happy to write one.
Okay, that makes sense. I'll email her this afternoon.

questions.prompt: What are the speakers mainly discussing?
options: Whether the student should go to a marine station
How the student did in a genetics course
What kind of fieldwork a lab is doing
Who should write a letter for the student
questions.explanation: The student asks for a letter, and the professor suggests Dr. Petrova would be a better writer.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention the size of his lecture class?
options: To point out that many students ask him for letters
To suggest he knows little about her practical skills
To explain why he grades the exams in his course so strictly
To show that her grade was unusually high
questions.explanation: He implies that in such a large class he never saw how she works in a lab or in the field.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and his thesis advisor.

turns.text: Professor Castillo, I have a problem with my thesis. The city archive is closing for renovations until April, and I was going to use their council records.
Oh, that's bad timing. Which years were you looking at?
The nineteen-twenties, when the city built its first public parks.
Then you might not need the archive at all. The local newspapers covered council meetings in a lot of detail back then, and our library has them on microfilm.
Would those count as primary sources?
Definitely. Newspaper reports from the time are primary sources. You'd just want to note that a reporter was summarizing, not quoting the official record.
That's a relief. I'll go to the library tomorrow and start with nineteen twenty-two.

questions.prompt: Why does the student go to see his advisor?
options: He wants to change the time period he studies.
He needs directions to the city archive.
He cannot get the records he planned to use.
He does not know how to read microfilm.
questions.explanation: He explains that the archive holding the council records will be closed until April.

questions.prompt: What does the professor say about the old newspapers?
options: They are kept at the city archive until April.
They can serve as primary sources for him.
They quote the council records word for word.
They mostly cover parks built after the twenties.
questions.explanation: She says newspaper reports from the time are primary sources, though reporters were summarizing.

intro: Listen to a conversation between two students.

turns.text: Grace, can I ask you something? Are you still going to the Wednesday study group for organic chemistry?
Honestly, I've been thinking about quitting. Last week we spent the first hour talking about a concert.
Same here. I went home and hadn't solved a single problem. But I don't want to study alone either.
What if we started our own? Just the two of us, maybe one more person. We'd each do the practice set beforehand and only meet to go over the ones we got stuck on.
I like that. Should we tell the others, though? I don't want them to feel like we're abandoning them.
We can just say we need a slower pace for the reaction mechanisms. That's true, anyway.
Fair enough. Thursday after lab?
Thursday works.

questions.prompt: What are the students mainly discussing?
options: Going to a concert together after their lab
Forming a more focused group for studying
Comparing their answers on a practice set
Inviting new members to the Wednesday group
questions.explanation: Both are unhappy with the current group and agree to start a smaller, more focused one.

questions.prompt: What does the woman imply about what they will tell the group?
options: It is true but leaves out their main concern.
It will probably upset the other members.
It is an excuse that she does not believe.
It shows that they have fallen behind in class.
questions.explanation: She says the reason about pace is 'true, anyway,' though their real complaint is that the group wastes time.

intro: Listen to a conversation between two students working on a group project.

turns.text: Diego, did you see Lucas's email? He says he can't edit our documentary at home anymore.
Why not? I thought he had the editing software.
He did, but it was a free trial, and it ran out. The full version is really expensive.
Hmm. The media lab in the arts building has that same program on every computer. Students in our course can use it for free.
Right, but the lab's always packed the week before projects are due.
You can reserve a station online, though. If we book a three-hour block on Saturday morning, all three of us could work on it together.
That might actually be better. Lucas has been doing all the editing alone, and he's kind of overwhelmed.
Then I'll make the reservation tonight and let him know.

questions.prompt: What problem are the students discussing?
options: Their documentary is due earlier than they expected.
A group member has decided to drop the course.
The arts building is closed on Saturday mornings.
A group member can no longer use the editing software.
questions.explanation: Lucas's free trial of the editing software ran out, so he cannot edit at home.

questions.prompt: What will the man probably do tonight?
options: Buy the full version of the software
Edit the documentary by himself
Send an email to their instructor
Reserve a computer in the media lab
questions.explanation: He says he will make the reservation tonight and tell Lucas.

intro: Listen to a conversation between two students.

turns.text: Sam, you're a psych major too, right? I can only fit one more course next term, and I'm torn between statistics and the social psychology seminar.
I took stats with Professor Kowalski last year. Brutal. Weekly problem sets, and she grades every one.
That's what I've heard. The seminar sounds like a lot more fun.
It is. But didn't you say you want to work in Dr. Amari's lab next year?
Yeah, I'm applying in the spring.
Well, everyone in that lab runs their own data analysis. When I applied, the first thing they asked was which stats course I'd taken. And the seminar's offered every term anyway.
Hmm. So I could take the seminar later. Okay. Kowalski it is, then. Wish me luck.

questions.prompt: What are the speakers mainly discussing?
options: Which course the woman should take next term
How strictly Professor Kowalski grades her students
How to apply to work in a psychology lab
Why the man enjoyed the social psychology seminar
questions.explanation: The woman is choosing between statistics and a seminar, and the man helps her decide.

questions.prompt: Why does the man mention what the lab asked him when he applied?
options: To suggest she apply to a different lab
To explain why he chose the seminar
To warn her that the lab rarely accepts undergraduate students
To show that statistics would help her plans
questions.explanation: He points out that the lab cares about statistics, which matters because she wants to join it.

intro: Listen to a conversation between two students.

turns.text: Bianca, you work at the natural history museum on campus, don't you? I saw they're hiring tour guides.
Yeah, I've been giving tours for a year. You should apply. The pay's decent, and the hours are flexible.
Do I need to know a lot about fossils already? I'm an English major.
Not at all. Half the guides are from the humanities. There's a two-week training where you learn the main exhibits, and you shadow a guide before leading a tour yourself.
Is the training paid?
It is. But it's the first two weeks of the semester, every weekday afternoon. So you'd need to keep those afternoons free.
I have a seminar on Tuesday afternoons, though.
Then email the coordinator before you apply. Sometimes they let people do a Saturday session instead.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: A seminar the woman is taking on Tuesdays
A job the man is interested in applying for
A new exhibit about fossils at the museum
A training course designed for English majors
questions.explanation: The man asks the woman about the tour guide job at the campus museum.

questions.prompt: Why does the woman tell the man to contact the coordinator?
options: He does not have any background in natural history or fossils.
The museum may stop hiring guides soon.
New guides are not paid for training.
His class schedule conflicts with the training.
questions.explanation: He has a Tuesday afternoon seminar, but the training takes place every weekday afternoon.

intro: Listen to a conversation between two members of a campus chess club.

turns.text: Felix, bad news about the chess tournament. Someone else booked the student center ballroom for the same Saturday.
What? We reserved it in September.
Apparently our booking was never confirmed. The events office says the other group finished their paperwork first.
Great. We already have forty players signed up. Could we use classrooms instead?
I asked. The math building has three rooms free, but they're on different floors.
That's a nightmare for running the pairings. We'd be running up and down the stairs between rounds.
Or we move it a week later. The ballroom's free then.
Hmm. A few players might drop out, but honestly, I'd rather lose a few people than run a messy tournament. Let's email everyone tonight.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: Recruiting more players for a tournament
Choosing a floor in the math building
Solving a problem with a room for an event
Announcing the results of a tournament
questions.explanation: Their ballroom booking fell through, and they discuss classrooms or a later date.

questions.prompt: What is the man's attitude toward postponing the tournament?
options: He worries the ballroom will be taken again.
He agrees only if no players drop out.
He thinks the classrooms would work better.
He accepts that some people may not come.
questions.explanation: He says he would rather lose a few players than run a messy tournament.

intro: Listen to a conversation between two students.

turns.text: Chloe, have you decided about next year? You were choosing between a single room in Brookside Hall and the apartment with Maya.
Still deciding. The single is so convenient. It's right next to the science buildings.
But isn't it more expensive?
That's the thing. The apartment's about two hundred dollars cheaper a month, even with utilities. And I'd have a kitchen, so I could stop paying for the meal plan.
How far away is it?
About twenty minutes by bus. I've got early labs on Mondays and Wednesdays, though.
The bus starts at six, so you'd be fine. And with what you'd save, you'd hardly have to work weekends.
True. Okay, I'll tell Maya tonight that I'm in.

questions.prompt: What are the speakers mainly discussing?
options: How to get to early labs by bus
Whether the woman should quit her job
Which meal plan the woman should buy
Where the woman should live next year
questions.explanation: The woman is choosing between a single dorm room and an apartment.

questions.prompt: Why does the woman decide on the apartment?
options: It would cost her less overall.
It is closer to her science labs.
Her friend did not want to live alone.
The single room is already taken.
questions.explanation: The apartment is two hundred dollars cheaper a month, and she could drop the meal plan.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and his research supervisor.

turns.text: Dr. Achebe, I have some bad news about the camera traps at the creek site. The batteries in four of them died, so we lost almost two weeks of footage.
Two weeks. During the cold snap?
Exactly then. I'm really sorry. I can go out tomorrow and replace them, and maybe extend the study two more weeks to make up for it.
Replace the batteries, yes. But extending won't give us the same data. Animals behave differently once it warms up.
So the gap just stays there?
It stays, and we report it. Honestly, the failure is useful. The next team needs to know these units can't handle freezing nights.
I guess I was expecting you to be more upset.
Equipment fails. What matters is that you told me right away. Write up what happened in the field log tonight.

questions.prompt: Why does the student go to see Dr. Achebe?
options: To get permission to end the study early
To report a gap in the data he was collecting
To request new cameras for the creek site
To discuss how animals behave in the cold
questions.explanation: He tells her that dead batteries caused them to lose almost two weeks of footage.

questions.prompt: Why does Dr. Achebe reject the student's plan to extend the study?
options: Later footage would not reflect cold conditions.
The team cannot afford any more batteries.
The creek site will soon close to researchers.
The field log has to be completed before any more recording.
questions.explanation: She explains that animals behave differently once the weather warms, so extra weeks would not replace the lost data.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and her research supervisor.

turns.text: Dr. Whitfield, I wanted to update you on the memory study. We've only had nine participants in three weeks, and we need forty.
Hmm, that's slow. When are the sessions scheduled?
Weekday mornings, nine to noon. That's when the lab room is free.
That might be the problem. A lot of students have classes then, and the ones who don't are probably asleep.
I hadn't thought of that. But the room's booked in the afternoons.
What about evenings? It's open after six. I'd also post the study on the participant website, where students sign up for course credit.
Okay. I'll add evening sessions starting next week and get the posting up today.
Good. Let me know how the numbers look by Friday.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: How to reserve a lab room in the afternoon
What participants remembered in a test
How to get more people to join a study
Why the study's results were disappointing
questions.explanation: The student reports low participation, and the supervisor suggests ways to recruit more people.

questions.prompt: What does the supervisor suggest might be causing the problem?
options: Participants often forget their appointments.
The lab room is too small for most groups.
The sessions are held at an inconvenient time.
The study's description is hard to understand.
questions.explanation: He says many students have classes or are asleep during weekday mornings.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and an art history professor.

turns.text: Professor Duarte, for my final paper I'd like to write about the mural in the old train station downtown. The one that was restored last year.
Good choice. Have you been to see it since the restoration?
Not yet. I've mostly been working from photos online. Some of them are really clear.
Photos are fine for the composition. But you know the restorers found an earlier painting underneath, right? Parts of it were left visible on purpose.
Wait, really? None of the photos I've seen show that.
Most were taken before the work was finished. That's why I'd go in person. And the restoration team is still in town. They might be willing to talk to you.
That would change my whole argument. I was going to say the colors were all the artist's originals.
Then you'd better see them first.

questions.prompt: What are the speakers mainly discussing?
options: The history of the old downtown train station
The reasons the mural had to be restored
The sources the student should use for a paper
The student's interest in becoming a restorer
questions.explanation: The professor advises her to see the mural in person and talk to the restorers rather than rely on photos.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about the student's planned argument?
options: It focuses too heavily on the mural's colors.
It may be based on outdated information.
It should compare the two layers of paint.
It depends on interviews that are unreliable.
questions.explanation: The photos she used were taken before the restoration revealed an earlier painting, so her claim about the colors may be wrong.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teaching assistant for a physics course.

turns.text: Hi, Carmen. I missed the pendulum lab on Monday because I had the flu. Is there any way I can make it up?
Sorry to hear that. Are you feeling better now?
Much better, thanks.
Good. Well, another section does the same lab on Thursday at two. You could join them for that week.
Thursday at two? I have a history class until two fifteen.
Hmm. The lab runs until four thirty, and the pendulum experiment only takes about an hour. If you get there by two thirty, you'll have plenty of time.
Great. Do I need to tell the other TA?
I'll email him today so he expects you. Just bring your lab notebook and your safety glasses.

questions.prompt: Why does the student talk to the teaching assistant?
options: To move permanently to a Thursday section
To get help with the pendulum experiment
To explain why he will be late to history
To arrange to complete a lab he missed
questions.explanation: He missed Monday's pendulum lab because of the flu and asks how to make it up.

questions.prompt: Why is it acceptable for the student to arrive late on Thursday?
options: The experiment is much shorter than the lab period.
The other assistant always starts the lab late.
He has already finished part of the experiment.
His history class usually ends a few minutes before two.
questions.explanation: The lab runs until four thirty, but the experiment takes only about an hour.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a philosophy professor.

turns.text: Professor Osei, you wrote on my draft that it has 'no argument yet.' I'm a little confused. I spent pages on both positions about free will.
And you explained both very clearly. That's actually the problem. By the end, I still don't know what you think.
I guess I didn't want to pick the wrong side.
In philosophy, there isn't really a wrong side. There's only a weak defense of a side. Which position did you find more convincing while you were reading?
Honestly, the second one. The examples about choices made under pressure really stuck with me.
Then start there. Keep your summary of the first view, but treat it as the objection you have to answer.
So the paper doesn't get longer. It just takes a direction.
Exactly. Bring me a new introduction next week.

questions.prompt: Why does the student go to see the professor?
options: To ask which side of the debate is correct
To request more time to finish the paper
To understand a comment she wrote on his draft
To find more examples of choices under pressure
questions.explanation: He is confused by her note that his draft has no argument yet.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about the student's draft?
options: Its summaries of both views are unclear.
It needs to become considerably longer.
It defends the weaker of the two positions.
Much of it can be kept in the revised version.
questions.explanation: She tells him to keep his summary of the first view and use it as an objection to answer.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teaching assistant for a computer science course.

turns.text: Hi, Raj. I couldn't submit my programming assignment last night. The submission site kept giving me an error.
Yeah, the server went down around ten. You weren't the only one. We got about thirty emails.
Oh, good. I mean, not good, but does that mean it'll count as late?
No. The professor extended the deadline to midnight tonight for everyone. She posted an announcement this morning.
I haven't checked the course page today. So should I just submit it again tonight?
Yes, through the site, the normal way. And if you saved your code before ten, you might mention the time in a comment, just in case.
I finished around nine thirty, so I'll do that. Thanks.

questions.prompt: What is the woman's problem?
options: She lost the code she wrote for an assignment.
She missed an announcement about a new task.
She is unable to log in to the course page.
She could not turn in an assignment on time.
questions.explanation: The submission site gave her an error, so she could not submit her assignment.

questions.prompt: What does the teaching assistant tell the woman?
options: She should email her code to the professor.
Her assignment will lose a few points for being submitted late.
The deadline has been moved for the whole class.
The site will be down until tomorrow.
questions.explanation: He says the professor extended the deadline to midnight tonight for everyone.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and his research supervisor.

turns.text: Dr. Leclerc, I've finished six interviews at the farmers' market, but three of the vendors didn't want to be recorded. I took handwritten notes for those.
That's fine, and you were right to respect that. Did you note it on their consent forms?
Consent forms? They agreed to the interview, so I just didn't think about it.
The plan we filed with the review board says every interview would be recorded. If we're switching methods for some people, the board needs to know.
Does that mean I can't use those three interviews?
You probably can. It's usually a quick amendment. But until it's approved, keep those notes separate, and leave them out of your analysis.
Okay. Should I write the amendment?
Draft it, and I'll sign it. Then we'll see.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: The vendors' opinions about the farmers' market
The student's trouble finding people to interview
A recording device that failed during interviews
A procedural issue with some of the interviews
questions.explanation: Some interviews were not recorded, which differs from the approved plan and requires an amendment.

questions.prompt: What will the student probably do next?
options: Interview the three vendors a second time
Prepare a request to change the study's method
Throw away his handwritten interview notes
Include the handwritten notes in his analysis right away
questions.explanation: Dr. Leclerc tells him to draft the amendment, which she will sign.

intro: Listen to a conversation between two members of a hiking club.

If we cover his lunch and let him pick the trail, I bet he would. He's always complaining that we choose easy ones.

Sure. I'll text him right now.

questions.prompt: What problem are the students discussing?
options: The rental office has no vans available that day.
The trail they chose is too difficult for members.
No one on the committee is allowed to drive the van.
The hiking site is much too far away for a single-day trip.
questions.explanation: The rental office requires drivers to be twenty-one, and all committee members are twenty.

questions.prompt: What will the woman probably do next?
options: Reserve the van under her own name
Choose an easier trail for the trip
Ask the rental office for an exception
Contact a club member about driving

intro: Listen to a conversation between two students.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and an engineering professor.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and his research supervisor.
